doc_summary: A multi-author methodological guide to rigorously evaluating adversarial-robustness defenses, arguing for explicit threat models, adaptive adversaries, deep skepticism of one's own results, and sanity checks that expose broken evaluations. Its core stance is that passing weak or non-adaptive tests is nearly worthless evidence, and that evaluators must adopt the mindset of a motivated real adversary.

items.claim: prefers evaluation against adaptive adversaries who know the specifics of the defense over non-adaptive or zero-knowledge tests because passing weak tests says almost nothing about real-world robustness.
items.quote: Defending against non-adaptive attacks is necessary but not sufficient. It is our firm belief that an evaluation against non-adaptive attacks is of very limited utility.

items.claim: prefers applying the mindset of a future real adversary over running off-the-shelf tests with default settings because defaults are tuned to past setups and can silently fail on a new target.
items.quote: applying the same mindset that a future adversary would apply is the only way to show that a defense might be able to withstand the test of time.

items.claim: Distrusts a negative result (attack fails, defense looks robust) because it may reflect a flawed or poorly tuned test rather than true robustness, so failure to elicit a behavior is weak evidence.
items.quote: gradient masking may make optimization-based attacks fail but that does not mean that the space of adversarial perturbations decreased.

items.claim: prefers treating success as a negative goal that only survives sustained attempts to disprove it over accepting the absence of observed failure, because researchers easily fool themselves.
items.quote: Adversarial robustness is a negative goal – for a defense to be truly effective, one needs to show that no attack can bypass it.

items.claim: Validate your test harness itself by checking it succeeds on known-broken or intentionally-vulnerable targets, so that a null result is interpretable.
items.quote: This can be done by selecting alternate models that are either known to be insecure or are intentionally designed to be insecure, and verify that the new attack algorithm can effectively break these defenses.

items.claim: Use monotonicity and impossibility sanity checks (stronger attack or larger budget must do at least as well) as diagnostics, treating violations as evidence the evaluation itself is broken.
items.quote: Attacks that allow more distortion are strictly stronger than attacks that allow less distortion. If the attack success rate ever decreases as the amount of distortion allowed increases, the attack is likely flawed.

items.claim: In a setup, define a realistic threat model that models some actual adversary with stated goals, knowledge, and capabilities instead of an arbitrary or unfalsifiable one, because it makes the evaluation meaningful and falsifiable.
items.quote: Without a threat model, defense proposals are often either not falsifiable or trivially falsifiable.

items.claim: In a setup, assume the adversary is highly capable and knows the system's inner workings instead of relying on obscurity or secret details, because real attackers will not be constrained by the designer's assumptions.
items.quote: In general, the guiding principle of a defense’s threat model is to assume that the adversary has complete knowledge of the inner workings of the defense. It is not reasonable to assume the defense algorithm can be held secret

items.claim: Report per-example worst-case outcomes across all attacks rather than averages per attack, because aggregates hide that some method succeeds on a given instance.
items.quote: it is important to report attack success rate on a per-example basis instead of averaged over the entire attack.

items.claim: prefers diverse, carefully adapted attacks over many near-identical ones because redundant tests give a false sense of thoroughness.
items.quote: do not show a massive table with many similar attacks that have not been adapted to the defense. Instead, rather show a shorter table with a more diverse set of attacks that have each been carefully adapted and tuned.

items.claim: prefers using checklists as a list of known failure modes to think with rather than a procedure to follow blindly because mindless compliance is counterproductive.
items.quote: Blindly following the checklist without careful thought will likely be counterproductive: each item in the list must be taken into consideration within the context of the specific defense being evaluated.

items.claim: Flags open problem: gradient-free attacks currently fail on randomized models, so stronger attacks for that setting are needed.
items.quote: the state-of-the-art gradient-free attacks currently do not do well in this setting. (Future work on this challenging problem would be worthwhile.)
